And therefore, it's good to learn the skill of maintaining (for yourself, or for your group) one mental mode, inter alia, in which you're able to remember firmly the first-order effects. That feels like a fully general heuristic for ignoring second order effects? Second order effects matter more than first order effects all the time!

My steelman is that it's a good heuristic when there are intense illegitimate optimization pressures pushing towards making people believe the second order effects matter more than the first. But if that's actually your point then it feels unfair to apply it to AI2040 Plan A and Redwood's work on conceptual reasoning, where I expect these optimization pressures to be weak, and comparable in magnitude to illegitimate optimization pressures in the other direction.

The recipe is a mixture of ignoring and not-ignoring, the pluralism of framings (trying out different emphases on different parts of what you understand, seeing where that leads). It addresses the danger of systematic not-ignoring warping your thinking, in a way that ignoring straightforwardly won't. Exclusively ignoring and never growing up to start hearing what the adults are actually saying is a failure mode of this recipe, not its prescription. Just as permanently forgetting your inner child is a failure mode.

Like with [every other kind of intervention](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/CseMTXtQHynGR8S5k/every-point-of-intervention), a society as a whole can (and should) consider doing all of them at once. The low-hanging fruit can be collected if merely a substantial number of people quit in protest, and a substantial number of people try to make prosaic alignment/control go OK. It's worse if either is neglected too much, and so there doesn't need to be a choice. Flip a coin if you must.

Obviously posts on alignment difficulty exist, but I think it's quite rare that a post on the LW front page or a quick take is explicitly arguing for alignment difficulty (or for alignment optimism). The most recent one I can think of is EY's on catbelling.

Yes, step 1 is not actually irrelevant to step 2 - it is helpful in the short term while we get nice headlines and harmful in the long term when those headlines are forgotten and the remaining people working in AI are less supportive of coordination and less likely to be outspoken about risks.

But in the particular case where you know that your tweet about quitting due to the risks will get 100M views, yeah you should quit.
